Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Trump, Xi and Putin held an unprecedented trilateral in Shenzhen, pledging talks on nuclear risk and strategic stability as alliances recalibrate; a joint “peace declaration” omitted explicit references to Ukraine. 
• The International Court of Justice issued a landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during 2017 operations, the first such ICJ decision against a state. 
• The US and Venezuela signed a military deal less than a year after Maduro’s removal, signaling a sharp pivot in regional security ties. 
• Somalia expelled the UAE ambassador, accusing Abu Dhabi of violating its sovereignty amid escalating tensions. 
• South Korea’s top court ordered a retrial of ex-PM Han over an alleged martial law attempt, tightening legal scrutiny on insurrection. 
Why it matters: Shifts in great-power diplomacy, a historic genocide ruling, and fast-moving regional disputes are reshaping norms and alliances with knock-on effects for security and trade.

Armed Conflict & Security
• Putin vowed a “far more painful” response to Ukraine after a strike on the Crimean Bridge; reports suggest Kyiv used relay drones to circumvent connectivity limits. 
• The Israeli military conducted a ground operation in Gaza beyond the Yellow Line to target a tunnel, drawing Hamas accusations of a ceasefire breach. 
• Escalation around the Strait of Hormuz intensified, with Iran-linked attacks and US responses raising fears of a wider confrontation. 
• An air strike hit Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund headquarters amid continued Houthi barrages, underscoring cross-border risks. 
Why it matters: Multifront escalations—from Ukraine and Gaza to the Gulf—are heightening risks to civilians, supply chains and energy markets.

• Nvidia’s leadership transition drew scrutiny even as interim CEO Colette Kress sought to reassure staff and investors; analysts flagged allocation quirks and reporting delays. 
• A US consortium won rights to Kenya’s Mrima Hill critical minerals deposit, beating Chinese rivals in a strategic supply-chain win. 
• US initial jobless claims edged up to 203,000, suggesting a still-resilient labor market. 
• Next-gen battery maker Sila secured a major supply deal with Panasonic, signaling momentum for silicon anode technologies. 
Why it matters: AI exuberance, chip-sector volatility and critical mineral deals are reshaping capital flows, industrial strategy and market leadership.

• A mosque arson in Israel drew condemnation as a hate crime; Canada’s Tim Hortons faced backlash over a data-sharing deal tied to Israeli military-linked firms. 
• In the UK, four men were convicted of sexual assault and rape facilitated by the victim’s husband, underscoring online exploitation risks. 
Why it matters: Conflict accountability, migration tragedies, hate crimes and privacy concerns reveal widening human-rights fault lines needing legal and policy remedies.

Artificial Intelligence

• Canva added an AI “off” switch, while Apple’s Siri Recap and always-listening features sparked debate on ambient recording and privacy. 
• Major US school districts may ditch Google Search after Gemini-linked AI toggles, highlighting tensions over default AI in education. 
• DeepMind unveiled Gemini 4 Neon and Genie 4, and Blue Origin will launch Google’s AI server satellites in 2029 under Project Suncatcher. 
• Microsoft’s Satya Nadella warned of “unpatchable” infrastructure and urged adaptation as AI reshapes security and workforce planning. 
Why it matters: AI’s mainstreaming brings new capital, competitive dynamics, infrastructure demands and governance questions across schools, cloud, and security.

• A report alleged the Trump administration took 500+ actions weakening carcinogen protections, raising exposure risks amid rising early-onset cancers. 
• Trump withdrew his FDA nominee; the Senate shelved a vote on his NSF pick, reflecting mounting confirmation headwinds.

Why it matters: Regulatory shifts, contested therapies and new biomedical tools will influence public health outcomes and trust in institutions.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• A large study found today’s older adults maintain memory longer than prior generations, suggesting cohort-level gains in cognitive aging. 
• Research linked heightened inflammatory signaling to reduced thermogenesis with age; senescent macrophages and Gas6 pathways were implicated in osteoporotic and calcific aging processes. 
Why it matters: Decoding cellular senescence and age-related inflammation could yield interventions that preserve function and slow age-associated disease.

Climate & Environment
• Cooking emissions dominated London’s mealtime air pollution, while car use is forecast to rise 10% in the next decade, challenging air-quality goals. 
• EU experts backed bloc-wide restrictions on “forever chemicals”; El Niño painted Chile’s Atacama in blooms and contributed to damaging floods in the US Southwest. 
• Data center electricity demand could double by 2030, with AI workloads straining grids; COP31 draft text kept electrification goals but dropped fossil fuel references, irking vulnerable nations. 
• South Africa raced to replant centuries-old baobabs after an attempted export; new subsea research hubs aim to protect Florida’s corals under thermal stress. 
Why it matters: Policy gaps, climate extremes and infrastructure demand are testing resilience and the credibility of climate commitments.

Economy & Markets.title: Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You
Economy & Markets.text: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand. But what does that actually mean?Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.A personal brand is a discovery mechanismStrip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.Don’t write AI slopLinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.) And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.Hot takes, with cautionPosts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.” You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.A routine you can followPosting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.Write for the people a few steps behind youThe best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.—BrianIEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI AssistantTo help researchers search through the millions of peer-review publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library, IEEE has released a custom AI suite optimized for STEM literature. The suit allows users to search with natural-language queries and provides overviews with reference links. Read more here. Artificial Intelligence.title: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
Artificial Intelligence.text: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, Is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is SpeculativeRSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.The Game of Superintelligence How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might leadKey • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress1. Alan Turing1936Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.REALITY CHECK  Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm.2. I. J. Good1965Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”3. Backpropagation1986Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.4. Vernor Vinge1993Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”REALITY CHECK  Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess.5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky1990s–2000sBostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.6. Deep learning breakthroughs 2010sLarger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.7. The race to self-improving AI2020sDario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.8. Reality check 2020sFrançois Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.YOU ARE HERE2026AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES1. The Intelligence ExplosionAI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.2. Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”Explore the Superintelligence DebateIn a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.The Dangers of Chasing SuperintelligenceEven if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

Science & Technology.title: Lamborghini Proves There Doesn’t Need To Be a Compromise With the Temerario Spyder
Science & Technology.text: SummaryLamborghini unveils the Temerario Spyder, featuring its first-ever fully electric retractable hard top.Featuring a 907-horsepower twin-turbo V8 hybrid powertrain catapults the supercar from 0 to 62 mph in 2.8 seconds.An enlarged cabin and 13 driving modes ensure uncompromised comfort and performance.Lamborghini has officially unveiled the Temerario Spyder, marking 50 years of open-top series-production with another bold engineering milestone. A first for any Lamborghini Spyder, the supercar features a fully electric retractable hard top.Rather than relying on traditional hydraulics, the roof utilizes ten electric actuators to tuck vertically behind the seats. This packaging preserves the car’s weight distribution while lowering its center of gravity by three mm when stowed. The entire mechanism operates at near silence, taking 17 seconds to go up or down at speed of up to 31 mph. Underneath, torsional rigidity has been increased by six percent over its predecessor while reducing structural complexity. Power comes from a HPEV setup, mating its flat-plane 4.0 liter twin-turbo V8 with three electric motors. Revving to a screaming 10,000 rpm, the hybrid powertrain churns out a combined 907 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque, catapulting the car from 0-to-62 in just 2.8 seconds.Inside, the enlarged cabin gains space over its predecessor, comfortably fitting drivers up to two meters tall, complete with integrated neck warmers and an electronically adjustable rear window that lets occupants listen to the V8 sing. With 13 selectable driving modes, including a three-level Drift mode and quiet all-electric cruising, the Temerario Spyder proves that there doesn’t need to be a compromise when turning a coupe into a convertible. Art & Culture.title: A Look Back at Maison Martell’s Creative Exchange in Chanteloup
Art & Culture.text: Maison Martell invited four fashion visionaries to Château de Chanteloup earlier this fall. Serving as the base for a unique creative exchange, the historic estate, which the Cognac Maison has called home for decades, inspired discussions on heritage, craft, and, more importantly, future collaborations.The collective in attendance included Johannesburg-based multidisciplinary artist Rich Mnisi and Nigerian-American designer and image director Ugo Mozie, as well as New York-based designers Brandon Blackwood and Jacques Agbobly. Hailing from different areas of fashion, the experience aimed to bring them together under a shared mission of discovery, where they would find out what shapes their creative worlds.Before delving further into their own practices, the appointed “Swift Ones” explored the journey behind Martell’s cognacs, from the vineyard through to distillation, barrel-making and ageing. The group later took part in a blending experience, where they created their individual blends. The immersion also included the Signature Martell dinner at Château de Chanteloup, providing a gastronomic experience by three-Michelin-starred chef Alexandre Mazzia.The collective then joined heads for a group conversation led by Martell Culture Ambassador Ivie Ani. With the tour bringing heritage into perspective, they spoke about the stories that form their journeys. Reflecting on this, Mozie shared, “Every final expression is built through layers, people, process, material, time, and instinct. That is very similar to how I approach designing and styling; what you eventually see is the result of many different elements coming together with intention.”For Blackwood, an entrepreneur whose contemporary brand is built on visual identity, the experience was more about staying true to what makes you unique. “The brand has been around for generations, but it hasn’t lost what makes it special,” he said. “I think about that a lot as a founder: How to build something with a strong identity that people connect with but never stop evolving or challenging yourself creatively.”While the Swift Ones exchange helped to build relationships, it also set out to connect the Maison with contemporary culture and the people driving new ideas from a mutual respect for craft.
